rationale: Boron does not survive radical benzylic bromination: NBS oxidises and protodeboronates a boronic acid or its ester. The measured case borylated first and then brominated, carrying a free boronic acid through an NBS step and two more besides.

Any hydride strong enough to take an amide to an amine takes an ester with it. The archetypal chemoselectivity failure, and invisible to the competitor channel because the step is unimolecular and so has no second reagent to compete with.
As B 2 for a nitrile reduction: the reagent that takes the nitrile to the primary amine reduces the ester too.

Aluminium hydride reducing an ester reduces an amide as well. The direction matters -- a mild borohydride is selective for a ketone over an ester, which is why MC 6 carries no such row, but nothing selective for an ester over an amide is on the shelf.

A benzylic halide surviving an amide or sulfonamide N-alkylation would have out-competed the intended alkyl halide for the deprotonated nitrogen. Read on the *product* rather than the precursors on purpose: the intended electrophile's halide has left by then, so a halide still present is one the step did not mean to use.

An amine and an acyl chloride in one flask acylate before any palladium turns over. Only the acyl chloride is named: the amine is present by construction, since the template would not have fired without it, and naming it as well would match the intended nucleophile.

A free thiol poisons palladium: it binds the metal far more strongly than any substrate and the catalytic cycle stops. Invisible to both selectivity channels by construction, and not merely uncurated there -- each of them counts distinct *products*, and a poisoned catalyst makes none. Scoped by tag because this is a property of the catalyst and not of any one coupling, so one pattern covers all eighty-nine palladium rules and keeps covering the ninetieth. A thioether is not matched: it coordinates weakly and these couplings tolerate it.

A free trivalent phosphorus on the substrate competes with the catalyst's own ligand for the metal, which changes or destroys the active species. Same argument as B 7 and the same blind spot: there is no product to count. A phosphonate or phosphine oxide is four-connected and so not matched, which is the distinction that matters -- those are spectators.

Nitration of an azine, with the ring nitrogen ortho to the carbon nitrated. An azine ring is far too electron-poor for an electrophile to reach: the nitrogen withdraws from the ring and, under the acidic conditions these reactions need, is protonated as well, which deactivates it further. Read on the *product* because that is the only side that says where the electrophile went -- the precursor is the bare arene and the position is not yet decided. The aromatic nitrogen is tied to the substituted carbon by a path of aromatic bonds rather than looked for anywhere in the molecule, so a pyridine elsewhere on a large substrate does not block substituting a benzene ring. Three rows because a path has no variable length without recursive SMARTS, which no arm here allows; pyrrole-type nitrogen is excluded for free, being activating rather than deactivating. **Corrected, and the nitrogen is divalent on purpose.** A pyridone's ring nitrogen carries a hydrogen or a substituent and *donates*: the ring is activated like a phenol, and 2-pyridone brominates at C-3 with NBS, so `[nX2]` is what separates an azine from its oxo tautomer. A path rather than a ring here, because a carbon alpha to a pyridine-type nitrogen is electron-poor in a five-membered ring as much as in a six: C-2 of a thiazole is as unreachable as C-2 of a pyridine, and every diazine has such a position.

A Boc carbamate or a tert-butyl ester does not survive a strongly acidic medium -- both cleave to the free amine or acid, and the step delivers something other than what was asked for. One pattern covers both, which is why it is written on the acyl carbon rather than on the tert-butyl: a tert-butyl *ether* is far more robust and a Cbz survives acid, and neither is matched. Invisible to both selectivity channels by construction: the acid is the medium, not a named precursor, so nothing in the pot can be seen to cleave it, and a channel that counts distinct products cannot count a group that simply leaves.

An organic azide does not survive a Mitsunobu: the triphenylphosphine that drives the reaction reduces it by Staudinger, faster than the alcohol is activated. The collision is common now that click chemistry puts azides everywhere and the Mitsunobu is a workhorse. Invisible for the same reason as B 18 -- the phosphine and the azodicarboxylate are the reagents and neither is a named precursor, so there is nothing in the pot to compete with. The azide *anion* is not matched, being a legitimate reagent elsewhere, and a triazole is not either, the azide having already been spent.

An alcohol, phenol or carboxylic acid quenches the organometallic. A protic hydrogen quenches an organometallic before it can add. Invisible to both selectivity channels because the species that gets quenched is not in the pot: these templates name the alkyl halide, not the Grignard reagent made from it, so there is no molecule for the proton to react with and no product for either channel to count. Three rows and not one because `[OX2H1,SX2H1,NX3;H1,H2]` is refused at parse time -- "SMARTS clause spans multiple properties (H, X) and cannot be represented as independent masks" -- so the disjunction has to be split. **Deliberately the strictest row in this table**, and worth reading in `measure` mode first: excess Grignard will overcome a single protic site in practice, so a chemist would call this a cost rather than a wall. A carboxylic acid is the clear-cut case, being consumed and then attacked. **Moved onto `tag:carbanion`.** The row used to name the six Grignard codes explicitly; the directed-metalation rules MC 97a to MC 97c need exactly the same pattern, and an aryllithium is quenched harder than a Grignard, so the membership belongs beside the reactions rather than inside this row.

A diazene carrying a hydrogen on nitrogen decomposes to the arene and dinitrogen in seconds; diimide itself is not a compound at all. Two routes were built through phenyldiazene and two through diimide, each generated by deprotecting a stable acyl or Boc diazene that really is on the shelf -- so the deprotection step is the fault, not the starting material. An azo compound with no N-H is a dye and is not matched, which is the distinction that matters. A **non-isolable species**, and so a different kind of fault from every row above: not a reaction that fails, but a molecule the route hands on that does not exist as drawn. Both selectivity channels are blind to it for the usual reason -- each counts distinct products, and this *is* a product, just not of the structure claimed. Unscoped, because the fault is a property of the molecule and not of any template: no reaction may hand this on, and `on=precursors` reads it where a route would carry it forward. Found by a blind route judge, which flagged three such species in twenty-four pairs and was right about them -- while being wrong about eight of the eleven leaves it called unpurchasable, all of which are in the Enamine catalogue.

No organometallic can be made from a halide that carries an epoxide: the metal opens the epoxide rather than inserting into the carbon-halogen bond, so a glycidyl Grignard is not a reagent. The measured case asked for exactly that -- epichlorohydrin plus acetaldehyde -- and `FWD H 45` reported it clean, because epichlorohydrin *is* an alkyl chloride as far as that pattern can see. Oxetane and tetrahydrofuran are not matched: the three-membered ring is what makes the epoxide electrophilic enough to win. **Found by watching a price pick the wrong route.** With the selectivity price raised, the search preferred this step over the correct one, because the forward rule paired with it fires here and reports *one clean product* -- the cheapest verdict a step can get -- while the correct alternative was charged for the mixture it honestly makes. A too-permissive forward rule does not merely fail to catch a bad step; it actively recommends it, and raising the price amplifies that. Narrowing the forward left-hand side instead would need "an alkyl halide bearing no electrophile", which is a recursive pattern and so unavailable on every arm. Read on the *product*, where the surviving group is unambiguous, which is the same argument B 5 makes.

An enolisable aldehyde cannot be in the flask when an alkoxide is generated. The base deprotonates alpha to the carbonyl far faster than it deprotonates the alcohol, and what follows is aldol and Tishchenko chemistry rather than an ether. The measured case asked for the alkoxide of 6-hydroxyhexanal, which compounds the fault -- the nucleophile *is* the aldehyde -- but the row is written on any enolisable aldehyde in the step, because an aldehyde on the halide partner is destroyed just as surely. An unstabilised enol is not the species the bottle holds: it tautomerises to the carbonyl, and a catalogue carries the keto form, so refusing the enol costs no route the ketone cannot supply. Said positively because the subset has no recursive SMARTS to say "not conjugated to a carbonyl": the hydroxyl carbon must carry one sp3 carbon, and here the far carbon is a terminal methylene. B 33 is the substituted case. Measured against 100,000 Enamine rows: the blanket pattern [OX2H1]-[CX3]=[CX3] condemns 39 of them and every single one is stabilised -- vinylogous acids, tetronic acids, ascorbate-like lactones, fluorinated 1,3-diones -- while B 32 and B 33 together condemn none. Found by the alternatives report, not by reading the table: MC 79, retro alkene hydrogenation, offers C=C(O)CC1CO1 as a precursor of CC(O)CC1CO1 with sites 1, so the forward pattern calls it one clean product.

B 32 for an enol whose far carbon carries a substituent, which must be sp3 carbon. Both sides are pinned to sp3 carbon for one reason: every stabilised enol the catalogue actually sells is conjugated to a carbonyl, a nitrile or an arene on one of the two carbons, so requiring sp3 on both is the expressible form of "unstabilised". A one-row version requiring it on the hydroxyl carbon alone still condemned 5 of 100,000 -- hexafluoroacetylacetone, a dimedone-like cyclic 1,3-dione, a cyanoenol -- each stabilised from the far side. MC 79 offers CC(O)=CC1CO1.

An oxirene has never been isolated. It appears only as a matrix-trapped intermediate of the Wolff rearrangement, so a template that emits one has written a species no bottle holds -- and the catalogue agrees: 0 of 100,000 Enamine rows match. Cyclopropene, the all-carbon analogue, is a real compound with a real boiling point and is deliberately not covered; the ring is named by its oxygen rather than by its size because the subset has no r3. MC 79 offers CC(O)CC1=CO1, an oxirene, as a precursor of CC(O)CC1CO1.
